newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary closes largest ex-Yugoslav refugee camp.
newsitem.headline: Hungary closes largest ex-Yugoslav refugee camp.

text.p: Hungary closed its main camp for refugees from former Yugoslavia at Nagyatad near the Croatian border on Monday, transferring the remaining refugees to a smaller camp in the east of the country to cut costs.
Nagyatad, a disused military barracks, was first opened in 1991 to house Croats and ethnic Hungarians fleeing the Yugoslav Army's shelling of the Croatian towns of Osijek and Vukovar.
Bosnians began arriving in 1992 and now account for all but a handful of the 500 or so remaining refugees.

Most are now waiting either to return to Bosnia or to go to third countries and last week they threatened to go on hunger strike rather than uproot to unfamiliar accommodation even further from former Yugoslavia.
"I can't understand why they're moving us again - I just want to go home," said 78-year-old Mandolina Zelic, a Bosnian Croat who has spent the last four years in Nagyatad.
Bela Jungbert, head of the Hungarian government's Refugee Office, told Reuters the move was purely a financial decision.

"The capacity of the camp is over 2,000 and we don't have at the moment more than 500," he said. "Half of these will leave for the U.S., Canada or Bosnia and there is no reason to have such a large camp."

Jungbert said most of the refugees who wished to return had been waiting for travel documents from the Bosnian and Croatian governments since last December and would be repatriated as soon as these papers were forthcoming.

Around 800 have so far returned from the Nagyatad camp, mainly as a result of the efforts of a German charity "Survive the War" which by-passed the Sarajevo authorities and obtained letters of invitation directly from local authorites in Bosnia.
The camp's director, Lajos Horvath, told Reuters by telephone from the train carrying the refugees to their new quarters that all had boarded peacefully.

"People are less tense, I think they've accepted that they have to move," he said. "But I think the sadness of leaving the contacts they made in Nagyatad will hit them when they arrive at the new camp."
